thread.title_full: Nuclear missiles once kept Soviets at bay, now part of historic site - NewsBreak

author: The Dakota Scout / Scouting Yesterday
title: Nuclear missiles once kept Soviets at bay, now part of historic site - NewsBreak
text:
By The Dakota Scout / Scouting Yesterday ,
7 hours ago WALL, S.D. – Hundreds of intercontinental ballistic missiles housed in the plains of western South Dakota helped keep the Cold War cold, on the ready to launch nuclear warheads at a moment’s notice.
But 25 years ago this week, the Air Force crews installing a missile at silo Delta-09 weren’t upgrading the arsenal — they were adding the newest artifact to the developing Minuteman Missile National Historic Site .
Russian officials were allowed 30 days to inspect the installation.
A glass dome east of Wall covers the silo, which stores a 57.6-foot, 70,000-pound missile, absent its former nuclear payload. It took eight years of planning between the Air Force and the National Park Service to get the missile back in the silo, according to the Rapid City Journal .
“We need to let people know that for 30 years, as they drove down Interstate 90, they were actually going through a war zone,” said William Supernaugh, superintendent of Badlands National Park , who oversaw the development of the historic site. “While there weren’t any signs of damage and destruction, the potential was there. This would have been ground zero in a nuclear exchange.”
Construction of South Dakota’s deployment area began on Sept. 11, 1961, according to the National Park Service. Completed in September 1963, work went on seven days a week, three shifts per day building the 165 structures — 15 launch control facilities hardwired to 150 nuclear missile silos.
A thousand Minuteman missiles would be fully operational by the end of 1967, located at six deployment areas throughout the Midwest.
By 1973, all Minuteman sites received upgraded Minuteman IIs, the missile seen at the historic site today. Carrying a 600-pound W56 nuclear warhead, yielding 1.2 megatons of explosive power — 66 times the destructive power of the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima — every Minuteman II could strike the Soviet Union within 30 minutes.
Visitors to the historic site that opened in 2003 can also see the nearby Launch Control Facility Delta-01, where, 31 feet beneath the prairie, Launch Control Center crews from nearby Ellsworth Air Force Base manned the nuclear trigger at all times, with constant above-ground support. Two launch keys were placed 12-feet apart to prevent any one person from turning both at the same time, and the armed launch crews were authorized to shoot to prevent sabotage or unauthorized launches.
As the Cold War came to an end, the 1991 Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty resulted in the removal of approximately 80 percent of strategic arms then in existence, according to the National Park Service. A former Minuteman launch control facility and silo are also preserved near Cooperstown, N.D., as North Dakota State Historic Sites.
The historic site’s missile isn’t the first Minuteman to be without a warhead in the state, though. In 2017, readers learned that freedom of information filings by the Rapid City Journal and others resulted in the release of documents related to a 1964 Air Force “Broken Arrow” event — an accident involving a nuclear weapon.
Occurring near Vale, S.D., the released documents detailed the explosive separation of the missile and its payload after inspection crews used a screwdriver to check a fuse instead of the specified insulated fuse puller, shorting the circuit in the process.
The nuclear warhead fell 75 feet to the silo floor — without detonating.
